items.title: Affine spaces over a real vector space and displacement vectors
items.statement:
Let $V$ be a real vector space, with addition $+$, zero $0$, and additive
inverses ([[def-vector-space]]). An **affine space over $V$** is a nonempty set
$A$ together with a map

$$+\;:\;A\times V\longrightarrow A,\qquad (p,v)\longmapsto p+v,$$

such that

1. $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$; and
2. for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$.

The map in clause 1 is the **action** of $V$ on $A$. The unique vector supplied
by clause 2 is written $q-p$ and is called the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**;
thus $q-p$ is the unique $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$. An affine space over the real
vector space $V$ is also called a **real affine space modelled on $V$**, and
then $V$ is its **space of displacements**.

The following identities are consequences of the two clauses, with the displayed
justification:

- $p+(q-p)=q$ for all $p,q\in A$: this restates the defining property of $q-p$
  in clause 2.
- $p-p=0$ for all $p\in A$: taking $q=p$ in the previous display gives
  $p+(p-p)=p=p+0$, and clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,p)$ gives
  $p-p=0$.
- $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$: this is clause 1.
- $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ for all $p,q,r\in A$:
  $p+\bigl[(q-p)+(r-q)\bigr]=\bigl[p+(q-p)\bigr]+(r-q)=q+(r-q)=r=p+(r-p)$,
  so clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,r)$ identifies the two vectors.
- For each $p\in A$ the map $V\to A$, $v\mapsto p+v$, is a bijection: for
  every $q\in A$, clause 2 supplies $v=q-p$ with $p+v=q$, proving
  surjectivity; it is injective because
  $p+v=p+w$ gives $p+(v-w)=\bigl[p+v\bigr]+(-w)=p+w-w=p=p+0$, so clause 2
  applied to $(p,p)$ gives $v-w=0$, that is, $v=w$.

**Affine coordinate systems.** Suppose $V$ is $4$-dimensional and
$E:\mathbb R^4\to V$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).
For a chosen point $o\in A$, define

$$x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),\qquad p\in A .$$

This is a bijection $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$: it is injective and surjective because
$E^{-1}$ is a bijection and $p\mapsto p-o$ is a bijection of $A$ with $V$ by the
bijection just proved, applied with that $o$. Such maps are the **affine
coordinate systems on $A$**; clause 2 is exactly what makes them well defined,
because it is clause 2 that attaches to each ordered pair $(o,p)$ a unique
displacement $p-o$.
items.strategy: The uniqueness clause (b) is what makes q-p well defined. The identities follow from the action axioms and uniqueness: p+(q-p) = q is the defining property of q-p; p-p = 0 and p+0 = p come from p+0 = p; and p+[(q-p)+(r-q)] = [p+(q-p)]+(r-q) = q+(r-q) = r = p+(r-p) gives (q-p)+(r-q) = r-p by uniqueness. For each p, v |-> p+v is surjective by (b) and injective because an equality p+v = p+w and the action axioms give p+(v-w) = p = p+0, so v-w = 0 by (b) applied at (p,p).

items.title: Lorentz forms of inertia (3,1,0) on a 4-dimensional real vector space
items.statement: Let V be a 4-dimensional real vector space. A Lorentz form on V is a symmetric bilinear form eta: V x V -> R that is nondegenerate (both radicals are {0}) and has inertia (3,1,0): in some (equivalently, by Sylvester's law of inertia, in every) basis diagonalizing eta there are exactly three positive diagonal entries, exactly one negative diagonal entry, and no zero diagonal entry. The associated quadratic form is q(v) := eta(v,v). The pair (V,eta) is called a Lorentz vector space of signature (-,+,+,+).
items.strategy: Nondegeneracy is the statement that the radicals vanish; for finite-dimensional V it is equivalent to invertibility of the matrix of eta in any basis and hence to the absence of zero diagonal entries in every diagonalizing basis (the radical is the kernel of the associated map V -> V*, so its dimension is dim V minus the rank). The inertia (3,1,0) is the Sylvester normal form diag(I_3,-I_1,0_0) of the definition of definiteness/inertia; Sylvester's law makes it basis-independent. No positive-definite structure on V is assumed.

items.title: Timelike, null, spacelike and causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space. A vector v in V is timelike if eta(v,v) < 0, null (or lightlike) if v is nonzero and eta(v,v) = 0, spacelike if eta(v,v) > 0, and causal if it is timelike or null. The zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike. The sign of eta(v,v) is the causal character of v. The pairing eta itself is written <v,w> := eta(v,w) when no confusion arises. Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.
items.strategy: The classification is by the sign of the real number eta(v,v); the three alternatives eta(v,v) < 0, eta(v,v) = 0, eta(v,v) > 0 for v nonzero are mutually exclusive and exhaustive by trichotomy of the order on R, and the zero vector is excluded from the null case by definition.

items.title: Every Lorentz form admits an ordered basis with matrix diag(-1,1,1,1)
items.statement: Let eta be a Lorentz form on a 4-dimensional real vector space V. There is an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V with eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab} for all a,b. Such a basis is called eta-orthonormal; in every eta-orthonormal ordered basis exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the count is the inertia (3,1,0) of eta.
items.strategy: Sylvester's law of inertia supplies a basis in which the matrix of eta is the normal form diag(I_p,-I_q,0_r) with (p,q,r) the inertia of eta. The definition of a Lorentz form gives (p,q,r) = (3,1,0), so the matrix is diag(1,1,1,-1); reindexing the basis puts the single negative entry in the first slot and yields diag(-1,1,1,1). Since inertia is independent of the diagonalizing basis, every eta-orthonormal basis exhibits the same count.

items.title: eta-orthogonality and orthogonal complements in a Lorentz vector space
items.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.
items.strategy: Bilinearity gives that S^perp is closed under addition and scalar multiplication (each condition eta(.,s) = 0 is linear), and the containments and the equality S^perp = (span S)^perp follow by linearity in the second argument. The final sentence is witnessed by the classification: any nonzero null vector v satisfies eta(v,v) = 0, so v lies in v^perp.

items.title: Time orientation, future and past timelike/null/causal vectors, and the closed cones
items.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.
items.strategy: Well-definedness rests on the components lemma: T has exactly two components, so 'a choice of one of them' names a definite pair {C^+,C^-}. The claimed properties of the closures (convexity, the intersection {0}, and exclusivity of the future and past causal sets) are proved in the components lemma via the orthonormal coordinate description {v^0 >= |v_vec|} and {v^0 <= -|v_vec|} of the two closed cones.

items.title: The timelike set has exactly two convex components, described in orthonormal coordinates
items.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$
items.strategy: In the orthonormal basis, eta(v,v) = -(v^0)^2 + sum_i (v^i)^2, so eta(v,v) < 0 iff |v^0| > |v_vec|, which is the displayed union; the two sets are disjoint and nonempty (e_0 lies in the first, -e_0 in the second). Convexity of T_+: for u,w in T_+ and t in [0,1], (tu+(1-t)w)^0 = t u^0 + (1-t) w^0 > t|u_vec| + (1-t)|w_vec| >= |t u_vec + (1-t) w_vec| by the triangle inequality; T_- is handled by applying this to -v. Convex sets are path-connected, and T_+ and T_- are open (they are the preimages of (0,inf) under the continuous maps v |-> v^0 - |v_vec| and v |-> -v^0 - |v_vec|). Since T is the disjoint union of two nonempty relatively open connected sets, it is disconnected and these are its two components: any connected subset of T lies in one of them, because a connected subset meeting both would give a separation, while a path in T cannot change the sign of the continuous function v^0 (which is nowhere zero on T) by the intermediate value theorem. The closures are computed by continuity of v^0 -/+ |v_vec|; their intersection consists of vectors with v^0 >= |v_vec| and v^0 <= -|v_vec|, hence of 0 alone. Finally, any two orthonormal bases are related by a linear isomorphism, and the components of T are intrinsic to eta, so the coordinate description agrees with the components up to the naming of T_+ and T_-.

items.title: Oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (the spacetime primitives)
items.statement:
An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.
items.strategy: The definition is a structure specification: the affine action, the form, the orientation and the time orientation are separately defined objects, and the definition only bundles them and fixes the terminology (events, displacement, interval, causal relations). Well-definedness of the bundled data requires the existence and uniqueness statements supplied by the cited items: affine coordinates are available by the affine-space definition, the orthonormal basis needed later exists by the orthonormal-basis lemma, and the two components of the timelike set needed to choose C^+ exist by the components lemma. The translation invariance claim follows from the affine axioms: displacements are unchanged by translations, and translations have identity linear part, so they preserve eta, the orientation and C^+.

items.title: Inertial frames and inertial charts of the affine Minkowski model
items.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.
items.strategy: Well-definedness requires the existence of eta-orthonormal bases (orthonormal-basis lemma) and the possibility of making them future and positively oriented (existence lemma below). The transition formula follows from the definitions: if e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b, then for p = o + sum_a x^a e_a one has p = o' + sum_a x'^a e'_a with x' = M^{-1}(x - x(o')), because applying E'^{-1} to the displacement identity p - o' = (p-o) + (o-o') gives exactly that expression; that x' = 0 iff p = o' is then immediate.

items.title: Existence of future-oriented inertial frames at every event
items.statement: In every oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (A,V,eta,C^+) and for every event o in A there exists an inertial frame with origin o; consequently inertial charts are defined at every event. Explicitly: start from any eta-orthonormal ordered basis (f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3) of V; if f_0 is not in C^+ then replacing f_0 by -f_0 makes the first vector future (because the timelike set is the disjoint union of C^+ and C^- and eta(-f_0,-f_0) = eta(f_0,f_0)); the resulting ordered basis has some orientation class, and if that class is negative (det M = -1 relative to the fixed orientation) then replacing e_1 by -e_1 (or interchanging e_1 and e_2) produces a positively oriented ordered basis, without destroying eta-orthonormality and without changing the first, future vector.
items.strategy: Apply the orthonormal-basis lemma to get f_0,...,f_3. Since eta(f_0,f_0) = -1 < 0, f_0 lies in the timelike set T = C^+ disjoint-union C^-, so exactly one of f_0, -f_0 lies in C^+. Negating a basis vector preserves eta-orthonormality because eta is bilinear and (-1)^2 = 1, and negating one vector changes the orientation class by the sign of the change-of-basis matrix, which is -1; hence at most one further negation (or the interchange of two vectors, also of determinant -1) makes the ordered basis positively oriented while preserving eta-orthonormality and the future first vector. The origin o is appended freely since frames are allowed any origin.

items.title: The affine atlas makes the Minkowski model a smooth 4-manifold diffeomorphic to R^4
items.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ be one inertial chart. Give $A$ the **transported topology**
in which a set $U\subseteq A$ is open exactly when $x(U)$ is open in
$\mathbb R^4$; this is the unique topology making $x$ a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^4$. Then:

1. $A$ is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological $4$-manifold.
2. The one-chart family $\{(A,x)\}$ is a smooth atlas, so $A$ is a smooth
   $4$-manifold, and $x$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^4$ carrying its
   standard smooth structure.
3. Every affine chart of $A$, that is, every map $y(p)=Mx(p)+b$ with $M$ an
   invertible $4\times4$ real matrix and $b\in\mathbb R^4$, and in particular
   every inertial chart, belongs to the same smooth structure, and its
   transition with $x$ is the smooth diffeomorphism $u\mapsto Mu+b$ of
   $\mathbb R^4$, with inverse $u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-b)$.
4. The transported topology and the smooth structure do not depend on the choice
   of the initial inertial chart $x$.
items.strategy: For (i): x is by construction a homeomorphism A -> R^4; R^4 is Hausdorff, second-countable and locally Euclidean, and each of these properties transfers along a homeomorphism (separate points by preimages of disjoint open neighbourhoods; pull back a countable basis; use x itself as a global coordinate chart). For (ii): a one-chart family vacuously satisfies smooth compatibility, so {x} is a smooth atlas; the maximal atlas it generates is the smooth structure, and in this structure the coordinate representation of x is the identity, so x is a diffeomorphism onto R^4 equipped with the standard structure. For (iii): if y = M x + b is an affine chart, then y is a homeomorphism for the same topology and the transition y o x^{-1} is the map u |-> M u + b, whose components are polynomials of degree at most 1 in the coordinates; linear maps and constant maps of R^4 are smooth, and sums of smooth functions are smooth, so y o x^{-1} is smooth (one can differentiate componentwise using the algebra of total derivatives and the theorem that continuous partial derivatives imply total differentiability). Its inverse u |-> M^{-1}(u-b) is again affine and smooth, so y belongs to the same smooth structure; every inertial chart has this form by the transition formula of the frame definition. For (iv): if x' is another inertial chart, then x' = M x + b for an affine map of the displayed form, so the topologies transported by x and x' coincide and the two suggested one-chart atlases generate the same maximal atlas.

items.title: The tangent space of the affine Minkowski model at any event is canonically V
items.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the smooth structure of [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], and
let $p\in A$. A smooth germ at $p$ is the equivalence class of a smooth real function on an
open neighbourhood of $p$, where representatives agreeing on a smaller
neighbourhood are equivalent ([[def-germ-of-a-smooth-function-at-a-point]]).
For such a germ $[f]$ define

$$\Phi_p(v)([f]):=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}f(p+tv),\qquad v\in V .$$

Then $\Phi_p:V\to T_pA$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$ onto the tangent space
$T_pA$; in particular $T_pA$ is canonically identified with $V$, independently
of any chart. If $x$ is an inertial chart and
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$, then the coordinate derivations satisfy
$\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.
items.strategy: Well-definedness: for a smooth germ [f] the curve c(t) := p + t v has, in the inertial chart x, the coordinate representation x(p) + t u with u = E^{-1} v, hence is smooth; therefore f o c is smooth near 0 and the derivative at 0 exists. Differentiation of products of smooth functions gives Phi_p(v)([fg]) = f(p) Phi_p(v)([g]) + g(p) Phi_p(v)([f]) by the product rule, so each Phi_p(v) is a derivation, and Phi_p is linear in v by the chain rule applied to t |-> x(p) + t u. Injectivity: if Phi_p(v) = 0 and x is an inertial chart at p with coordinates x^a, then applying Phi_p(v) to the germs x^a - x^a(p) gives v^a for each a, so v = 0. Bijectivity: the coordinate derivations partial_0,...,partial_3 form a basis of T_pA, so dim T_pA = 4 = dim V, and an injective linear map between these spaces is an isomorphism. Canonicity: the curve t |-> p + tv is defined by the affine structure alone, so Phi_p does not depend on the chart; the final display follows from the coordinate computation in the chart.

items.title: The oriented volume form epsilon and the permutation symbols of an inertial frame
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let (o;e_0,...,e_3) be an inertial frame. For v_0,...,v_3 in V let [v_j^a] be the 4x4 matrix whose j-th column lists the coordinates of v_j in the ordered basis (e_0,...,e_3), and define epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3) := det([v_j^a]) in the sense of the determinant of a square matrix. Then epsilon is an alternating 4-linear form on V, called the oriented volume form of the model. Its components in the inertial frame are the permutation symbols epsilon_{abcd}, with epsilon_{0123} = +1 and epsilon_{abcd} the sign of the permutation taking (0,1,2,3) to (a,b,c,d) (zero if two indices repeat). The raised components are epsilon^{abcd} := eta^{aa'} eta^{bb'} eta^{cc'} eta^{dd'} epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}, where eta^{ab} is the inverse of the matrix eta_{ab}; epsilon^{0123} = -1. The spatial permutation symbol epsilon_{ijk} for i,j,k in {1,2,3} is defined by epsilon_{123} = +1 together with alternation.
items.strategy: epsilon is the determinant of the coordinate matrix of (v_0,...,v_3); the determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns, hence epsilon is an alternating 4-linear form. Its components in the frame are by definition the determinant values, i.e. the permutation-sign symbols; epsilon^{0123} computes to eta^{00}eta^{11}eta^{22}eta^{33} epsilon_{0123} = (-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1) = -1 because the inverse metric is diagonal in an eta-orthonormal frame. Well-definedness of epsilon as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used, is proved in the frame-independence lemma.

items.title: The oriented volume form is independent of the positively oriented inertial frame
items.statement:
The alternating $4$-linear form $\epsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]] does not depend on the inertial frame
used to define it. Explicitly, if $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and
$(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ are inertial frames with
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$ for the change-of-basis matrix $M$, then $\det M=+1$
(both ordered bases are positively oriented), and the coordinate matrices $X$,
$X'$ of any tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in the two frames satisfy $X'=M^{-1}X$,
so that $\det X'=\det(M^{-1})\det X=\det X$. Consequently
$\epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$ for every inertial frame, $\epsilon$ is the unique
alternating $4$-linear form on $V$ taking the value $1$ on every positively
oriented $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis, and in every inertial frame the
raised component $\epsilon^{0123}$ equals $-1$.
items.strategy: From eta(e'_a,e'_b) = eta_{ab} and e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b one gets the matrix identity M^T eta M = eta; taking determinants and using det eta = -1 gives (det M)^2 = 1, so det M = +1 or -1, and the orientation clause selects det M = +1. The coordinate columns of a fixed tuple in the two bases are related by X' = M^{-1} X, so multiplicativity of the determinant and det(M^{-1}) = (det M)^{-1} give det X' = det X; this is exactly the frame independence, and it also shows the normalized value 1 on the frame itself. Uniqueness of the normalized alternating 4-linear form is the uniqueness clause for the determinant as a normalized alternating multilinear function, transported to V by the coordinate isomorphism E. The raised component computation is the diagonal evaluation given in the definition.

items.title: SI units and coordinate conventions of the special-relativity framework
items.statement:
This framework fixes the following SI coordinate and unit conventions for the
oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and its inertial
charts ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

1. **Adopted conversion constant.** The framework uses a positive constant $c$
   with unit metre per second, $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, interpreted as the
   **speed of light in vacuum** under the framework's light postulate. In SI
   its numerical value is exactly $299\,792\,458$ by the definition of the
   metre (BIPM, *SI defining constants*, table row $c$). This exact unit
   convention does not prove that the ideal-light model describes nature;
   measurements and realizations of units still have uncertainty.
2. **Coordinates.** In every inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ define the
   coordinate-time map $t:A\to\mathbb R$ by $t(p)=x^0(p)/c$, with unit second
   $\mathrm s$, and assign unit metre $\mathrm m$ to every $x^a$. An **at-rest
   line of this frame** is $s\mapsto o+cs e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3r^ie_i$, $s\in\mathbb R$,
   for fixed spatial coordinates $(r^1,r^2,r^3)$ in metres; its coordinate
   time is $s$. Interpreting coordinate-time differences as readings of
   synchronized ideal clocks on these lines is a physical assumption stated
   in the clock postulate, not a consequence of assigning units.
3. **Metric components.** The matrix $\eta_{ab}=\eta(e_a,e_b)$ in the frame is
   $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with **dimensionless** entries. Thus
   $I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)=-(\Delta x^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(\Delta x^i)^2$
   carries unit $\mathrm m^2$.
4. **Proper time of a straight segment.** For a timelike displacement $q-p$,
   the affine straight segment is $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$, $s\in[0,1]$. Define its
   positive **proper-time length** as

   $$\tau:=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}.$$

   It has unit second, since $c^{-1}$ converts the square-root interval in
   metres into seconds. This length is positive even if the segment is
   oriented toward the past; a physical advancing clock uses future orientation.
5. **Kinematic bookkeeping.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval
   with parameter $\tau$ in seconds, and let $\gamma:J\to A$ have $C^2$
   coordinates $y=x\circ\gamma:J\to\mathbb R^4$
   ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). With
   $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$, require $U(\tau):=E(y'(\tau))\in C^+$ and
   $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. This is the **proper-time normalization** used here for
   units; the general construction of a proper-time parameter is developed
   later. The **four-velocity** is $U:J\to V$, with components $U^a=(y^a)'$
   and unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$. The **four-acceleration** is
   $\mathcal A=E(y''):J\to V$, with unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$.
   For a positive constant mass parameter $m$ in kilograms, define
   **four-momentum** $P=mU:J\to V$, with unit
   $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, and **energy measured by this frame**
   $\mathcal E=cP^0=-c\eta(e_0,P):J\to\mathbb R$, with unit joule
   $\mathrm J=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$. The equality follows from
   $\eta(e_0,P)=-P^0$. These are definitions for dimensional bookkeeping;
   the physical particle interpretation and dynamics belong to later pages.
6. **Temporal-coordinate convention.** Replacing $x^0$ by $t=x^0/c$ pulls
   the interval expression back to $-c^2(\Delta t)^2+\sum_i(\Delta x^i)^2$.
   Thus $g_{tt}=-c^2$ has unit $\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$, the spatial
   components remain dimensionless, and mixed time-space components have unit
   $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$ (and equal zero in this inertial chart). Formulas
   must be transformed when changing this convention.
7. **Natural units.** A presentation with $c=1$ identifies temporal and spatial
   units by this conversion factor; it requires an explicit restoration table
   for $c$. It does not assert that the SI numerical value of $c$ is $1$.

**Status.** These are conventions and dimensional bookkeeping for the model.
The SI numerical value of $c$ is exact by unit definition; the physical
interpretation and applicability of the model remain adopted and empirically
testable. SI unit status does not make a quantity primitive in the theory.
items.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalization (x^0 = ct rather than t), the unit of each component, and the dimensional interpretation of the interval, of proper time along a timelike straight segment and of the derived kinematic quantities, all relative to the adopted model and its inertial charts. The dimensional statements follow by inspection of the inertial coordinate expressions out of the diagonal form of eta, and the warning about the temporal-coordinate convention records where the components change dimension.

items.title: Adopted inertial covariance of the model equations
items.statement:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

The condition $\det L=1\ne0$ makes $L$ invertible by
[[thm-operator-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]. Fix $p_0\in A$; then
$F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ by the affine condition, and the map
$r\mapsto p_0+L^{-1}(r-F(p_0))$ is its inverse, so $F$ is a bijection.

For clarity, the induced transformation of tensors has the following precise
meaning. The **algebraic dual** $V^*$ is the vector space of linear maps
$\alpha:V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).
For integers $r,s\ge0$, a **type $(r,s)$ tensor** is a map
$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$ linear in each argument; write
$\mathcal T^r_s(V)$ for their vector space with pointwise operations
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]). A **tensor
field** here is an assignment $T:A\to\mathcal T^r_s(V)$; each particular
model specifies its tensor types, domains and required regularity. Its
transformed field is defined by

$$(F_*T)_{F(p)}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s):=T_p(\alpha_1\circ L,\ldots,\alpha_r\circ L,L^{-1}w_1,\ldots,L^{-1}w_s).$$

This is well defined since $F$ is bijective and all slot maps are linear;
for a restricted domain $D\subseteq A$ the new domain is $F(D)$. In particular
scalar fields transform by composition with $F^{-1}$ and vector fields by
$v_p\mapsto Lv_p$ at $F(p)$, since $\alpha(Lv_p)=(\alpha\circ L)(v_p)$.

Adopt the assumption that every solution configuration of each specified
mechanical or electromagnetic model is carried to a solution of that same
model by relabelling events with $F$ and applying the displayed transformations
to its fields and displacements. This is the meaning of **covariance** here;
which equations and admissible configurations constitute a model is specified
when that model is introduced.
items.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: the item records the adopted formulation (affine Minkowski geometry with a fixed orientation and future cone) and the adopted covariance of the framework's model equations under future- and orientation-preserving eta-isometries of V. The maps are characterized by their defining properties rather than by a named group; the group structure, factorization and algebra of these maps are established on the Lorentz-transformations page. The exposition must state the scope limitation that covariance is a property of the specified model equations and neither proves the model nor selects dynamics.

items.title: Adopted ideal-clock and ideal-vacuum-light interpretation
items.statement:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and
$\gamma:I\to A$ a curve. Choose an inertial chart $\chi$ with
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Require
$y:=\chi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ to be $C^1$ on the interior of $I$,
with its derivative extending continuously to any included endpoints, where
it is the one-sided derivative. Define the displacement-valued derivative by
$\dot\gamma(s):=E(y'(s))\in V$ and require $\dot\gamma(s)\in C^+$ everywhere,
including such endpoints. This derivative is chart-independent: a second
chart has coordinates $\widetilde y=M^{-1}(y-\chi(o'))$, so its
parameter derivative is $M^{-1}\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$, while its basis map
is $E'=EM$; their product is $E\,\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$.

An **ideal clock on this curve** has a reading map $\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$
in seconds, specified up to an additive constant, with, for all $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(\dot\gamma(s),\dot\gamma(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

The integrand is positive and continuous on $[a,b]$: the coordinate derivatives
are continuous, $\eta$ is a finite bilinear expression, and the square root
is continuous at every positive argument, as follows from
$|\sqrt r-\sqrt q|=|r-q|/(\sqrt r+\sqrt q)$ for $r,q>0$.
Thus [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] applies to this compact interval
and gives a well-defined Riemann integral. The reading rule contains no
additional acceleration-dependent correction (**clock hypothesis**); it does
not require $C^2$ regularity or an acceleration to exist. This is an adopted
physical interpretation of the length integral, not a proof about real clocks.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are the oriented
straight lines parametrized by $\ell:\mathbb R\to A$,
$\ell(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$, where $p\in A$ and $v\in V$ is future null;
increasing $\lambda$ specifies their future direction. In an inertial chart
$\chi$ their coordinate map is

$$\chi(\ell(\lambda))=\chi(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3).$$

Since the chart's time-axis vector is future, the cone description of
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] gives
$v^0=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$. With $t=\chi^0/c$ the spatial
coordinate velocity is $c(v^1,v^2,v^3)/v^0$ and has Euclidean magnitude $c$
in every inertial chart. The conversion constant is the same across charts;
its exact SI numerical value is a unit convention as specified in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], while the ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation is an adopted, empirically testable model assumption.
items.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: it fixes the physical interpretation of the mathematical objects (future timelike curves, future null straight lines) and the reading rule of an ideal clock, together with the exact scope of the idealization. The integral is well defined because the integrand -eta(x',x') is positive and continuous on a compact parameter interval for a future timelike C^1 curve; parametrization invariance and the resulting proper-time parametrization, as well as the general theory of worldlines, four-velocity and acceleration, are developed on the later worldlines-and-clocks page, which may not depend on this page by a forward edge; the postulate therefore states the reading rule for the model rather than a theorem about curves.

items.title: The Euclidean spatial structure and cross product of an inertial frame
items.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes the domains of $\delta$ and $\times$.
The Lorentz form, the fixed orientation of $V$, and the time orientation $C^+$
are data of the model independent of the named inertial frame
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). The Euclidean spatial structure instead
requires the choice of a time axis $e_0$; it is not an additional
frame-independent structure on the whole of $V$.
items.strategy: Since (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is eta-orthonormal, for w = sum_i w^i e_i one has eta(e_0,w) = 0 and eta(w,w) = sum_i (w^i)^2, so the restriction delta is positive definite and (e_1,e_2,e_3) is delta-orthonormal; positivity of eta(w,w) on S also shows S = e_0^perp. The vector product is well defined by its displayed coordinate formula, and the identity delta(w x z,y) = det(w,z,y) is Lagrange's identity for the cross product in an orthonormal basis; the norm identity is the same computation in coordinates. Frame dependence: a general eta-orthonormal frame has a different time axis e_0 and hence a different S, so the construction depends on the frame; the final sentence records that only eta is invariant.

items.title: Primitive and derived notions of the spacetime-primitives page
items.statement:
This remark records the primitive and derived status of the notions introduced
on the spacetime-primitives page, as required before the page's derived claims.
It is bookkeeping: it asserts no physical law and no empirical claim.

**Primitive mathematical structure of the model.** The quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: the affine space $A$ with
its action of $V$ and the displacement $q-p$, the Lorentz form $\eta$ of
signature $(-,+,+,+)$, the orientation of $V$ fixed as a positive ray of
$\Lambda^4V$, and the time-orientation component $C^+$ of the timelike set.

**Primitive physical interpretation and parameters adopted on this page.** The
physical event interpretation together with the covariance assumption
([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]); the ideal-clock and ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]); and the conversion
constant $c$, whose SI numerical value is exact by unit definition and whose
physical interpretation as the vacuum ray speed is adopted, as recorded in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. These are adopted assumptions
of the framework, not deductions.

**Derived (constructed, not adopted) on this page.** Displacements and
intervals; the causal classification of displacements; inertial frames and
their inertial charts ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); the smooth
structure of $A$ making it a smooth $4$-manifold and the canonical identification
$T_pA\cong V$; the oriented volume form and its components
([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); and the spatial Euclidean structure
and vector product of a named inertial frame
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). These are
mathematical constructions from the primitive structure, with the stated
frame-dependence where it occurs.

**Reserved for later development.** The general proper-time parametrization
theory, physical particle momentum and energy, charge, and force or matter
laws. The units item gives explicit kinematic definitions only for bookkeeping;
it supplies no dynamics or empirical particle identification. Later pages introduce their own adopted
premises and must repeat this status audit for them; a definition on a later
page is not made primitive by this page's conventions.

**Mathematical versus empirical status.** The mathematical statements of this
page concern only the stipulated geometry. They do not assert that the model
describes nature; the physical interpretation enters through the two adopted
postulates, whose empirical support would be evidence about the specified model
rather than a proof.
items.strategy: A status remark: it repeats, without proof obligations, the primitive/derived classification of the page's objects as required by the framework content model, and separates the mathematically constructed structure from the physically adopted interpretation. It carries no claim beyond that bookkeeping.

items.title: Worked affine transition between two inertial charts
items.statement: Worked computation of the transition between two inertial charts. Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with inertial frames (o;e_a) and (o';e'_a) and charts x, x', and write e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b with M invertible. Then for every event p, x'(p) = M^{-1}(x(p) - x(o')) = M^{-1} x(p) + b with b := -M^{-1} x(o'), so the transition is affine. Explicit 1+1-dimensional case: V = R^2 with eta(v,w) = -v^0 w^0 + v^1 w^1, o = o' = 0, e_0 = (1,0), e_1 = (0,1), and the boosted inertial frame e'_0 = (cosh r, sinh r), e'_1 = (sinh r, cosh r) for real r, which satisfies eta(e'_0,e'_0) = -1, eta(e'_1,e'_1) = +1, eta(e'_0,e'_1) = 0 and det M = cosh^2 r - sinh^2 r = 1 with M the matrix with columns e'_0, e'_1 in the e-basis. The transition matrix is M^{-1} = [[cosh r, -sinh r],[-sinh r, cosh r]], and x'(o) = 0, x'(x^{-1}(1,0)) = (cosh r, -sinh r).
items.strategy: Substitute the definitions: E'(u) = u^0 e'_0 + u^1 e'_1 = E(M u), so E'^{-1} = M^{-1} E^{-1} and x'(p) = M^{-1}(x(p) - x(o')). The 1+1 verification is by direct multiplication using cosh^2 r - sinh^2 r = 1: the metric identities for e'_0, e'_1 and the determinant-one orientation identity are finite computations, and the two displayed transition values follow from the matrix inverse written explicitly.

items.title: Worked causal classification of explicit displacements
items.statement:
Worked classification in an inertial frame of the model. Let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$x$ be an inertial chart with frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$. Vector coordinates mean $E^{-1}(v)\in\mathbb R^4$,
so $E^{-1}(e_a)=(\delta_a^0,\delta_a^1,\delta_a^2,\delta_a^3)$.
The chart $x$ itself acts on events in $A$, not on vectors in $V$. Computing with the components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$:

- $v=(1,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v^0=1=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, so
  $v$ is future null;
- $w=(2,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(w,w)=-4+1=-3<0$ and
  $w^0=2>1=\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, so $w$ is future timelike;
- $z=(1,2,0,0)$ has $\eta(z,z)=-1+4=3>0$, so $z$ is spacelike;
- $u=(-1,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(u,u)=0$ and $u^0=-1<0$, so $u$ is past null;
- $e_0=(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike with $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, and $-e_0$ is
  past timelike.

In particular no future causal displacement is spacelike, and the coordinate
descriptions $v\ne0$, $v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ (future causal)
and $v\ne0$, $v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ (past causal) reproduce
the sign classification. The nonzero condition excludes the cone vertex,
which belongs to both closed cones but is not causal.
items.strategy: All values are direct evaluations of the displayed diagonal form; membership in the future or past cone is decided by the sign of v^0 and the coordinate description of the closed cones proved in the components lemma. Each line is a finite arithmetic check, so the example is a complete computation from the definitions rather than a new result.

items.title: Worked orthogonal complement of a timelike displacement is positive definite
items.statement:
Worked computation. In an inertial frame of an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$, with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ in
the frame's coordinates, take the displacement

$$u=(2,1,0,0),$$

a future timelike displacement with $\eta(u,u)=-3$. A displacement
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ is $\eta$-orthogonal to $u$ exactly when
$-2v^0+v^1=0$, that is, exactly when $v^1=2v^0$. On that hyperplane

$$\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+(2v^0)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=3(v^0)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2,$$

which is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at $v=0$. Hence the restriction of
$\eta$ to $u^{\perp}$ is positive definite, and every nonzero displacement
orthogonal to a timelike displacement is spacelike.
items.strategy: Evaluate eta(u,.) = 0 and expand the quadratic form in the coordinates; positivity and the vanishing locus are read off the sum 3(v^0)^2 + (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2, completing the worked computation from the definitions.

items.title: The orthogonal complement of a null vector need not be positive definite
items.statement:
Statement refuted: "for every nonzero displacement $u$ of a Lorentz vector
space the restriction of $\eta$ to $u^{\perp}$ is positive definite"
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).
items.strategy: Direct computation with the displayed diagonal form: eta(u,u) = -1 + 1 = 0; expanding eta(u,v) = 0 solves the orthogonality condition; expanding eta(v,v) shows the restriction is positive semidefinite with kernel span(u), which refutes positive definiteness.

items.title: The causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space are not closed under addition
items.statement: Statement refuted: 'the set of causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space is a linear subspace, in particular closed under addition'. Counterexample: in an inertial frame with eta = diag(-1,1,1,1), let u = (1,0,0,0) and w = (-1,9/10,0,0). Then eta(u,u) = -1 < 0 and eta(w,w) = -1 + 81/100 = -19/100 < 0, so both u and w are timelike (u future, w past); but u + w = (0,9/10,0,0) has eta(u+w,u+w) = 81/100 > 0 and is spacelike. Moreover -u is causal but not future causal, so the future causal set is not closed under negation either. Closure of the full causal set under addition therefore fails; the future causal cone is closed under addition of future causal vectors, and that distinct statement belongs to the causality page.
items.strategy: Evaluate the diagonal form on the displayed vectors: the two timelike verifications and the spacelike value of the sum are finite arithmetic. The sentence about the future cone records that no claim is made here about sums of future causal vectors; that closure is proved later.

items.title: Worked component signs of the oriented volume form
items.statement:
Worked computation of the components of the oriented volume form in an inertial
frame with $\epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=+1$. The covariant components are the
permutation signs: $\epsilon_{0123}=+1$;
$\epsilon_{0213}=-1$, the sign of a single transposition;
$\epsilon_{2301}=+1$, the product of the two transpositions $(0\,2)$ and
$(1\,3)$; $\epsilon_{3210}=+1$, the product of the two transpositions $(0\,3)$
and $(1\,2)$; and $\epsilon_{abcd}=0$ whenever two of the indices coincide.
Raising all indices with the diagonal inverse metric gives
$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=-1$. For
the spatial symbol, $\epsilon_{123}=+1$, $\epsilon_{213}=-1$,
$\epsilon_{312}=+1$, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two spatial indices coincide.
items.strategy: Each value is a determinant or permutation-sign computation in the displayed frame, using the definition of the volume form; the raised component is the single nonzero diagonal term of the sum, as computed in the definition; the spatial symbol is the three-dimensional restriction of the same product with the frame's positive spatial orientation.

items.title: The Lorentz form is not an inner product
items.statement: Statement refuted: 'the Lorentz form eta of a Lorentz vector space is an inner product, i.e. a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form'. Counterexample: let (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an eta-orthonormal basis, whose existence is the orthonormal-basis lemma. The vector e_0 is nonzero but eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 < 0, so eta is not positive definite and hence is not an inner product; consequently eta does not induce a norm, and the positive-definite inner-product theory (Cauchy-Schwarz, norms, orthogonal projection) cannot be applied to eta without additional argument.
items.strategy: A single evaluation refutes positive definiteness: e_0 is nonzero and eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 by the definition of an eta-orthonormal basis. The definition of an inner product requires positive-definiteness, so the refutation is immediate.

items.title: Worked construction of a future-oriented inertial frame from an arbitrary orthonormal basis
items.statement:
Worked example of the sign and orientation adjustments. Let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space, fix any
origin $o\in A$, and let
$(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ be any $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis of $V$. Its first
vector is timelike. Set $g_0:=f_0$ if $f_0\in C^+$ and $g_0:=-f_0$ if
$f_0\in C^-$, and set $g_i:=f_i$ for $i=1,2,3$. This makes $g_0$ future while
preserving orthonormality. The time-axis reversal, when needed, has
change-of-basis matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and determinant $-1$,
so it flips the orientation class; retaining $f_0$ leaves that class unchanged.

If $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ is positively oriented, retain it. Otherwise replace
$g_1$ by $-g_1$ (or interchange $g_1$ and $g_2$); this flips the orientation
class, preserves orthonormality and leaves the future vector $g_0$ unchanged.
Together with $o$, the resulting basis is an inertial frame. In particular, a
past-directed, negatively oriented starting basis needs only the time-axis
reversal, giving $(o;-f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$. This is the explicit construction of
[[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]].

**Two-dimensional illustration.** In the two-dimensional analogue with
$A=V=\mathbb R^2$ with its translation action, $o=(0,0)$,
$\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1$, standard orientation (a basis is positive when
its coordinate determinant is positive), and future timelike set
$C^+=\{v:v^0>|v^1|\}$, take
$f_0=(-1,0)$ (past timelike) and $f_1=(0,1)$ (spacelike). Then
$-f_0=(1,0)$ satisfies $\eta(-f_0,-f_0)=-1$, $\eta(f_1,f_1)=+1$ and
$\eta(-f_0,f_1)=0$, and $-f_0$ is future; so $(-f_0,f_1)$ is an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis with future first vector, and the change of basis has
determinant $-1$. If the original pair was the negatively oriented one, the
pair $(-f_0,f_1)$ is positively oriented and is an inertial frame of the
two-dimensional analogue of the model.
items.strategy: Use the defining properties: negating a vector preserves eta-orthonormality and changes the change-of-basis determinant by the factor -1; the timelike set is the disjoint union of C^+ and C^-, so exactly one of f_0, -f_0 is future. The 1+1 example is checked by direct evaluation of the displayed diagonal form.
